title: Incremental Learning of Vision-Language Models via Task Subspace Projection and Dynamic LoRA
shortTitle: Incremental Learning of Vision-Language Models via Task Subspace Projection and Dynamic LoRA
abstract: Recent pre-trained vision-language models often encounter a Multi-Domain Task-Incremental Learning (MTIL) scenario in practice, where a set of classes of multi-modal tasks arrive incrementally. Due to privacy concerns and memory constraints, MTIL with pre-trained models encounters forgetting of knowledge from old tasks, degradation of zero-shot transfer capability, and underfitting of new-task knowledge. To overcome these challenges, previous MTIL methods attempt to learn a discriminative cross-task identification (CTI) module and an effective new-task adaptation (NTA) module. However, current CTI modules suffer from severe task confusion between seen and unseen tasks, and NTA modules cannot adaptively balance the performance and parameter cost while incorporating task-specific knowledge. To alleviate the above dilemmas, we propose an effective and efficient TSP-DLoRA method for MTIL, which consists of Task Subspace Projection (TSP) and Dynamic Low Rank Adapter (DLoRA) modules. Specifically, our TSP module includes a task identifier classifier based on task-specific subspaces and a feature projection strategy that can determine the identifier associated with samples from both seen and unseen tasks. Our DLoRA improves the knowledge adaptation from new tasks by dynamically assigning Low Rank Adapter (LoRA) across transformer layers based on the task distributions. Experimental evaluations across 11 datasets, using three performance metrics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/FerdinandZJU/TSP-DLoRA.

title: Mem2Fair: Online Fairness Control for Text-to-Video Generation via Fair Memory
shortTitle: Mem2Fair: Online Fairness Control for Text-to-Video Generation via Fair Memory
abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce systematically unfair demographic outcomes when prompts leave protected attributes unspecified. For example, prompts describing nurses without specifying gender may disproportionately generate videos depicting female nurses. Mitigating unfairness in T2V generation is particularly challenging: training-based methods that modify model internals require architecture-specific access and risk disrupting temporal consistency, while sampling-based methods often incur costly pre-deployment video generation. We present the first conditional online approachability formulation of attribute-level fairness for T2V generation. Building on this formulation, we introduce Mem2Fair, a plug-and-play framework that maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory. Using generated videos at inference time as feedback, Mem2Fair selects prompt-level attribute interventions based on the deviation from each concept's prescribed fairness target, without training or separate pre-deployment sampling. Experiments demonstrate that Mem2Fair consistently improves fairness over the unmodified generator and existing baselines across multiple demographic attributes, prompt settings, and target distributions, while maintaining comparable prompt-video alignment and video quality. We further demonstrate its effectiveness on commercial black-box T2V models.

title: Neural Dual Bounds: Valid-by-Construction JGLP Warm-Starts for MAP and Constrained MAP
shortTitle: Neural Dual Bounds: Valid-by-Construction JGLP Warm-Starts for MAP and Constrained MAP
abstract: We present Neural Dual Bounds, a calibration-free framework that produces deterministic upper bounds for MAP inference in probabilistic graphical models using a single neural-network forward pass. The framework trains a network to output the edge messages of a mini-bucket style upper bound on a given join-graph decomposition in a self-supervised manner by directly minimizing a smooth dual objective. The output of this network can be used at test time to warm-start a standard JGLP optimizer. Across diverse benchmarks, this warm start yields dual gaps that are orders of magnitude tighter than those from zero initialization, with the largest gains in the early-iteration regime. We also apply our framework for the constrained MAP (CMPE) task, where neural warm starts with test-time adaptation are comparable to the adaptive baseline on Bayesian networks and achieve the tightest dual gaps, by one to two orders of magnitude, on the grid and segmentation families.

title: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective
shortTitle: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective
abstract: Selecting context subsets is increasingly important in modern LLM inference, yet what makes a subset effective remains unclear. We study this question in the controlled setting of few-shot demonstration selection. We examine a hypothesis that demonstrations should collectively provide task-relevant information needed by a target query. Assuming that the query representation provides a useful proxy for these requirements, we formulate selection as sparse reconstruction and instantiate it with Residual Explanation Search (RES), a Matching-Pursuit-style diagnostic procedure. Across seven benchmarks and eight open-weight LLMs, no retrieval objective is universally best. RES outperforms MMR in 34 of 56 model--dataset pairs, with its clearest advantage on sentiment tasks, suggesting that query-conditioned collective reconstruction may capture useful complementarity that pairwise dissimilarity misses. Relevance-based retrieval remains strong on template-heavy reasoning benchmarks, while all retrieval methods underperform zero-shot prediction on average on StrategyQA, where a solution-reconstruction analysis is consistent with the query not exposing the required external knowledge. Target-model hidden states further show that retrieval objectives interact differently with representation spaces: middle-layer representations generally favor similarity retrieval, whereas last-layer representations are often stronger for residual- and diversity-based selection. These findings support a conditional, representation-dependent account of context subset quality rather than a universally superior selector.

title: Can an Agent Rethink What It Knows? Selective Scene Memory Updates in a Changing World
shortTitle: Can an Agent Rethink What It Knows? Selective Scene Memory Updates in a Changing World
abstract: Task configurations in factories, warehouses, and everyday physical environments change over time. Physical AI systems therefore need to incorporate new facts into scene memory while preserving valid information about equipment, objects, and operating constraints. We study updates to this parametric semantic-memory layer and present a joint evaluation of correction and preservation under finite update budgets. At fixed current fact count and memory parameter count, the protocol combines independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success. Using a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA, we evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets on four-field synthetic semantic configurations. In two exposure-matched history conditions, increasing the budget from eight to 32 updates raises joint success from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15%, respectively, while exact obsolete-value outputs fall from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero. Constant32, which matches preparation steps but repeatedly trains on unchanged content during the first 32 events, achieves higher early joint success at eight steps (53.65%); at 32 steps, it reaches 85.42%, below both changing-history conditions. These results distinguish rapid correction under a small budget from simultaneous correctness of the new fact and the other three facts after further training. For both changing histories, most cases remain jointly correct at all subsequent measured points from step 16 onward. Output analysis shows that short-budget failures primarily retain the old value; repeated training on the new fact together with the other current facts progressively replaces these obsolete answers.

title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
shortTitle: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
abstract: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

title: Beyond Alignment: Supervising the Generator for EEG-to-Image Reconstruction
shortTitle: Beyond Alignment: Supervising the Generator for EEG-to-Image Reconstruction
abstract: Visual brain decoding translates neural activity into human-interpretable images. While recent EEG-to-image reconstruction methods rely on aligning EEG signals with pretrained visual embeddings to condition an image generator, we empirically demonstrate that stronger cross-modal alignment do not translate into comparable gains in reconstruction quality. This indicates that improving the input condition alone is insufficient; the generative process itself requires explicit supervision. Although Representation Alignment (REPA) offers a solution by guiding diffusion transformers with pretrained vision encoder features, we find that EEG-conditioned generators struggle to follow these fixed targets. To address this mismatch, we introduce generation-derived supervision (GDS): an image-conditioned teacher that translates static image-encoder features into the internal representation space of a diffusion transformer. Our EEG-conditioned student generator closely tracks these dynamic targets during denoising, discarding the teacher at inference. Evaluated on THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG, our approach consistently outperforms conditioning-centric baselines, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity.

title: Continuous Lower-Limb Joint-Angle Estimation from sEMG and IMU: The Conditional Value of Cross-Activity and Cross-Subject Data under Update-Matched Controls
shortTitle: Continuous Lower-Limb Joint-Angle Estimation from sEMG and IMU: The Conditional Value of Cross-Activity and Cross-Subject Data under Update-Matched Controls
lab: Conamur / Institute of Neuroscience, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of California, Santa Barbara
abstract: Intent-driven exoskeleton control needs a continuous, causal estimate of the wearer's joint kinematics and an answer to a second question: whose data should train the estimator for a new user? Borrowing the user's recordings of other activities, or other users' recordings of the same activity, is usually evaluated as "more data" versus "less data," which confounds the information a source carries with the optimizer updates it adds and hides negative transfer behind averages. We separate these effects for hip, knee, and ankle angle estimation from high-density sEMG and an IMU across six locomotion activities on all ten participants of a public dataset. A compact residual causal TCN-GRU decoder is frozen, and an update-matched replay control prices every added source against the same number of updates on the user's own data. A user's own other activities raise $R^2$ from 0.722 to 0.788, of which +0.048 is information beyond replay; stair descent is a reliably harmful donor and sit-stand-walk a reliably beneficial one. Other users' same-activity data help while the user has only the target activity ($G_\mathrm{T} = +0.053$) and half as much once own other-activity data exist ($G_\mathrm{W} = +0.028$); at full calibration, donor value collapses after one to two target records. Per-target gains from the two sources correlate, and leave-one-participant-out gates recover most of the cross-subject value only at low calibration. Data value is hierarchical, state-dependent, and directional; the bottleneck is deciding, without test labels, when to transfer.

title: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
shortTitle: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers specialized capabilities to language-model agents, but its cross-domain effects on interaction remain unclear. We investigate how OPD reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across mathematics, ALFWorld, and $τ^2$-bench, focusing on reasoning, actions, and observation acquisition. General-reasoning supervision reduces mathematical tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while increasing accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%; code-interpreter supervision improves household actions and retail queries. In contrast, ALFWorld supervision reduces $τ^2$-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6%, accompanied by frequent tool calls that violate user-information dependencies. To address negative transfer using only source-domain training trajectories, we explore selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL. Retaining the top 95% of positions raises $τ^2$ accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.

title: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models
shortTitle: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models
abstract: For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player's own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.

title: Size-Matched Nulls Reveal What Block Ablation Measures in MambaVision
shortTitle: Size-Matched Nulls Reveal What Block Ablation Measures in MambaVision
abstract: Hybrid vision backbones interleave Mamba state-space mixers with self-attention, and a block's role is usually probed by removing it and measuring the damage. We test what that measurement means in MambaVision. On all 50,000 ImageNet validation images and three model sizes, every block ablation is paired with a size-matched null, the same perturbation with its channels shuffled or their signs flipped. In top-1 accuracy and in true-class rank, real and null damage are nearly indistinguishable in absolute terms: pooled over the blocks of MambaVision-T, the content effect lies within [-0.044,+0.016] percentage points (90% interval). Two attention-only controls show that the test detects content, with real ablations worse than their nulls by up to 4.2 points in DeiT-Small and 1.0 point in Swin-T. Part of MambaVision's near-equivalence reflects how little damage its blocks do (0.11--0.34 points on average, against 1.7 and 2.1). Scaled by damage, its content share is comparable to Swin-T's in accuracy, lower in rank, and far below DeiT-Small's: single-block damage in MambaVision is small and mostly positional. Ablation also hides what blocks carry together: removing all blocks of one type compounds damage to 3.7--8.4 times the sum of single effects, far more than size-matched nulls, including nulls that keep the alignment between the blocks' perturbations; for adjacent pairs, aligned nulls reproduce most of it. Freezing input-dependent selection in all Mamba mixers shows that it accounts for 20--32% of the Mamba contribution, mainly through the B and C projections. We turn these results into a protocol for causal attribution in hybrid networks.

title: Learning Graph-Conditioned Predictors in Weight Space
shortTitle: Learning Graph-Conditioned Predictors in Weight Space
abstract: The same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Yet fast graphless models typically treat topology as additional evidence supplied to a globally shared predictor. This assumes that structure augments the available information, rather than determining how node attributes should be interpreted. We introduce SCOPE (Structure-COnditioned PrEdictor), in which a small generator maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. The base predictor, basis, and generator remain shared across all nodes, while the resulting transformation adapts how attributes are processed in each relational environment. Once fingerprints are cached, inference requires only a forward pass and no online message passing. This design combines context-specific specialization with global parameter sharing, compact low-rank adaptation, and message-passing-free inference. On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights with raw positional signals yields clear gains over supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Further results under a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and in teacher-free graph classification show that the mechanism extends beyond a particular distillation setting. These findings establish graph structure not only as predictive evidence, but as context that determines the predictor used to interpret that evidence.

title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
shortTitle: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

title: Auditory-Feedback-Conditioned Flow TTS for Implicit Lombard Adaptation
shortTitle: Auditory-Feedback-Conditioned Flow TTS for Implicit Lombard Adaptation
abstract: Conventional text-to-speech (TTS) systems can lose intelligibility in noise environments because they cannot adapt to environmental changes. However, humans tend to increase their vocal efforts in noisy environments, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. Building on an auditory-feedback Lombard TTS, we investigate whether a pretrained Flow-based TTS can learn acoustic adaptation directly from auditory feedback without explicit prosodic control. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feedback and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback are extracted from the noise-corrupted waveforms and injected into the Flow-matching condition for utterance refinement and causal block-level updates. We assess feedback benefits across prompting and noise conditions using plain/Lombard prompting, prompt-switching controls, and paired-finetuning. Experiments show that while finetuning provides strong robustness under in-domain conditions, auditory feedback yields additional cue-dependent benefits that generalize to unseen noise. Moreover, stronger power/F0 tracking alone does not guarantee better speech intelligibility or quality.

title: dit.xpu : Taming DiT Sparse Inference on Mobile SoCs
shortTitle: dit.xpu : Taming DiT Sparse Inference on Mobile SoCs
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) enable on-device image generation and editing but incur high attention costs at high resolutions. Existing sparse attention reduces computation, yet dynamic sparsity introduces preprocessing and irregular data accesses that poorly fit mobile NPUs. We present DiT.XPU, a sparse DiT inference framework for heterogeneous mobile SoCs. DiT.XPU combines tile-aligned sparse attention with anchor-based error compensation by exploiting slowly varying dense-sparse output residuals across denoising steps. Heterogeneous XPU collaboration overlaps NPU dense attention with GPU sparse calibration, while mask-guided dataflow reduces data transfers and layout conversion by overlapping data movement with computation. Across five DiT models on two Snapdragon smartphones, DiT.XPU achieves up to 1.56x end-to-end denoising speedup over the Hexagon-NPU backend and 11.5x attention-kernel speedup over the fastest alternative, while preserving generation quality close to dense attention. Code is available at https://github.com/IF-LAB-PKU/dit.xpu.

title: Distributed Shaping of Robot Swarms Through Spatial Moments of Arbitrary Order
shortTitle: Distributed Shaping of Robot Swarms Through Spatial Moments of Arbitrary Order
abstract: This paper shapes a swarm into a target pattern, such as a figure taken from an image, by controlling its spatial moments. The image is sampled into a reference configuration whose centroid and covariance set the position and principal spreads of the formation, while its higher-order moments, expressed in covariance-normalized (whitened) coordinates, encode the remaining shape. In contrast with geometric formation control, which prescribes distances, bearings, or relative positions between specific agents, this specification concerns the swarm as a whole and assigns no agent to a particular place. The key mechanism is orthogonalization in the swarm's own empirical inner product: projecting negative-gradient velocities onto the complement of low-degree polynomials sampled at the agents makes every higher-order correction preserve all lower-order moments exactly. The resulting hierarchical controller has lower triangular error dynamics and converges locally exponentially for any positive gains, so orders can be added without undoing those already achieved. A joint alternative regulates the higher moments together through a regularized Gauss--Newton step while preserving the centroid and covariance dynamics. We give bounds on the number of agents and sufficient conditions for regularity. Both controllers admit a distributed implementation that uses only relative positions and neighbor communication and retains local exponential convergence when estimation is sufficiently fast. In a distributed simulation on a sparse graph, 350 agents form an airplane from an unstructured swarm through moments up to order ten; the hierarchy reaches the full specification, while the joint law approaches it with smaller velocities.

title: B-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs
shortTitle: B-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs
abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD

title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
shortTitle: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.

title: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
shortTitle: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

title: Rethinking KV Caching for LLM Decode: Free-Space Optical KV Regeneration for Reduction of Memory Traffic
shortTitle: Rethinking KV Caching for LLM Decode: Free-Space Optical KV Regeneration for Reduction of Memory Traffic
abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) decoding repeatedly reads the historical key-value (KV) cache, making multi-head attention (MHA) memory-bandwidth-bound. Caching layer-input activations instead halves historical-cache storage and traffic, but requires regenerating KV from each cached activation. On digital accelerators such as GPUs, this regeneration takes far longer than fetching the activation from HBM. The KV regeneration overhead outweighs the savings from reduced memory traffic, shifting decode attention from a memory bottleneck to a compute bottleneck. We present OptiDecode, a hybrid optoelectronic decode-attention accelerator that regenerates historical KV using free-space optics and computes attention digitally. Projection weights remain resident on optical tiles, exploiting reuse across historical tokens for high-throughput optical regeneration. Scaling to large models introduces two challenges. First, distributing weights across tiles requires sending the same activations to every head group, while each readout die produces only partial KV. Activation replay shares one set of electrical-to-optical converters across head groups without costly broadcast. In-situ attention avoids transferring partial KV from readout dies to reducers by computing on them locally and exchanging only partial scores, probabilities, and partial outputs. Second, processing an activation chunk through all dependent stages takes longer than one activation-fetch interval. Chunk pipelining overlaps successive chunks so that OptiDecode sustains the HBM activation-fetch rate. OptiDecode demonstrates 1.92-1.99x decode-attention speedup over an ideal GPU KV-read baseline at equal peak HBM bandwidth (A100-B200), for 32K-token contexts across evaluated 30B-175B MHA models, approaching the 2x upper bound from halving historical memory traffic.

title: LC-ISP Benchmark: Learning Advanced ISP with Live and Capture Streams
shortTitle: LC-ISP Benchmark: Learning Advanced ISP with Live and Capture Streams
abstract: High-quality paired RAW-to-sRGB datasets are essential for data-driven ISP, yet existing datasets often rely on cross-device collection, causing misalignment and failing to faithfully reflect real capture conditions. We therefore introduce LC-ISP, a large-scale benchmark built from the intrinsic gap between a camera's live preview and offline capture streams. LC-ISP contains 53.9k spatially aligned groups, each comprising live RAW/live sRGB and multi-frame fused RGB/capture sRGB, and covers day, night, indoor, outdoor, and HDR scenes. It also provides capture-stream intermediates for modular supervision. We further develop a compact two-stage baseline that uses these intermediates as auxiliary targets. Under a 2.5-GFLOP budget for 448$\times$448 RAW inputs, it outperforms the strongest single-frame baseline by over 2 dB PSNR while improving texture, denoising, and color reproduction. LC-ISP supports realistic benchmarking, the design of supervision strategies, and the development of lightweight ISP models.

title: Generate, Align, and Restore: MLLM-Empowered Diffusion for Generalizable Low-light Image Enhancement
shortTitle: Generate, Align, and Restore: MLLM-Empowered Diffusion for Generalizable Low-light Image Enhancement
abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is essential to numerous vision applications operating under adverse illumination. Despite substantial advances, real-world nighttime enhancement remains challenging due to the scarcity of strictly aligned day-night pairs and complex degradations involving extreme darkness and heterogeneous artificial light sources, leading to fragile generalization. To overcome these challenges, we propose MrLIE (MLLM-empowered reference Low-light Image Enhancement), a novel reference-based unsupervised LLIE framework that synergizes the generative and reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with conditional diffusion. MrLIE employs the MLLM as a high-fidelity reference synthesizer and diagnostic critic, iteratively generating, diagnosing, and correcting normal-light references directly from degraded nighttime observations. Based on this, our method governs the enhancement process through two complementary mechanisms, in which a confidence offset module rectifies spatial-geometric inconsistencies for reference reliability and a structure-anchored injection scheme harmonizes aligned reference cues, low-light structural constraints, and ControlNet additive anchoring during the denoising process. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that MrLIE achieves superior perceptual quality, natural appearance, and robust generalization.

title: On Representational and Functional Alignment of Training Data Attribution Methods for Language Models
shortTitle: On Representational and Functional Alignment of Training Data Attribution Methods for Language Models
abstract: Existing approaches to training data attribution derive influence estimates from different sources of information, including gradients, model-internal states, and surface-level similarity. However, comparisons between attribution methods remain incomplete, often relying on indirect evaluations through downstream task performance. In this work, we introduce a framework for directly comparing methods along three dimensions: functional alignment, which measures correlation between full attribution vectors; representational alignment, which captures structural similarity of the representations underlying attribution; and cross-method predictability, which evaluates agreement on local pairwise ranking decisions. We observe strong representational and moderate functional alignment within paradigms. Alignment across paradigms is low and task-dependent, yet stable across models. Our results suggest that the similar downstream performance observed across paradigms in prior work can be attributed to agreement on the relative importance of documents, rather than to agreement on rankings of the full training data.

title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
shortTitle: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
shortTitle: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

title: Where Mixture Recognition Fails: An Ingredient-Level Audit of Unseen Combinations in SmellNet
shortTitle: Where Mixture Recognition Fails: An Ingredient-Level Audit of Unseen Combinations in SmellNet
abstract: An electronic nose must name every ingredient of a mixture, including combinations it has never measured. SmellNet, a public benchmark for this task, scores ingredients with a hit rate that is told how many each sample contains. We audit what this protocol hides. We hold out ingredient combinations from the SmellNet training data, evaluate four architectures (MLP, CNN, LSTM and a Transformer encoder) without revealing the ingredient count, and repeat the evaluation once on the official unseen split. Under the count-informed protocol, 90-96% of mixtures receive an ingredient that is absent, on our folds and on the official split alike. On our folds, every model identifies one ingredient reliably but the second rarely, and it completes the pair with a familiar training partner about twice as often as chance. On the official split, even the first-ranked ingredient is correct in only 29-46% of binary mixtures, often because a frequent training ingredient that is absent from every test pair is ranked first, and on its combinations that are truly absent from training no model names both ingredients in more than 1.2% of them. The failures fall on the same ingredients for every architecture, and a frequency correction only moves errors between ingredients. Mixture recognition is therefore limited by ingredients the models cannot separate and by a preference for frequent ingredients, not by the architecture, and it should be evaluated with set-level errors and without oracle cardinality.

title: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
shortTitle: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
abstract: Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability & computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
shortTitle: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

title: A Backdoor Trigger Is Legible in Fine-Tune Weights
shortTitle: A Backdoor Trigger Is Legible in Fine-Tune Weights
abstract: A backdoored language model behaves normally until a trigger phrase appears in its input. Every published method for recovering such a trigger runs the model. We show the trigger is legible in the weights alone: a static statistic reads a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward pass of the suspect, no data, no labelled population of poisoned models and no prior knowledge that a backdoor exists, and names one of the tokens of the trigger phrase as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.

title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
shortTitle: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

title: SAR-TopoGuard: Training-Free, Speckle-Aware Topological Verification for Structure-Preserving SAR-to-Optical Translation
shortTitle: SAR-TopoGuard: Training-Free, Speckle-Aware Topological Verification for Structure-Preserving SAR-to-Optical Translation
abstract: SAR-to-optical translators often synthesize detail that the radar measurement does not support, and pixel metrics alone cannot reveal it. We propose SAR-TopoGuard, a training-free inference-time layer for frozen generators: a stochastic sampler draws K candidates (Monte Carlo dropout for GANs, seed variance for diffusion), a speckle-aware verifier ranks them by gradient-magnitude correlation with the SAR input and a hallucination-frequency index, and a SAR-guided frequency gate admits high-frequency detail only where SAR edges support it. With all five hyperparameters frozen and three training seeds, we evaluate on 500 scene-disjoint SEN1-2 test patches, 500 patches of a held-out summer scene, and 200 cross-dataset SEN12MS winter pairs. The layer improves Pix2Pix by +0.060, +0.012, and +0.077 dB PSNR and by +0.0034, +0.0057, and +0.0135 SSIM, respectively (Wilcoxon p < 1e-6), and it improves CycleGAN and CUT on all three sets (+0.013 to +0.076 dB). It raises edge precision at the cost of edge recall (edge F1 -1.3% on the test set). On the latent diffusion model COP-GEN, it adds +0.33 dB (base) and +0.16 dB (Beta) on the winter set, the only set with dual-polarization SAR. An ablation shows that the gate produces the gain for MC-dropout GANs, whose candidates are nearly identical, whereas verifier selection contributes up to +0.26 dB for diffusion, whose samples differ. The layer has zero trainable parameters and adds 0.4 ms per patch beyond the K=5 generator passes.

title: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Visual Servo Control with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
shortTitle: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Visual Servo Control with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
abstract: We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise. Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor-Critic in the digital twin. A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates. We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch. Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound. Across conveyor speeds (27.9-41.8 mm/s), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1-1.4 mm (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.3-0.7 mm. These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
shortTitle: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
abstract: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

title: Generation of protein conformations using a simple inverted transformer
shortTitle: Generation of protein conformations using a simple inverted transformer
abstract: Molecular dynamics is an extremely powerful approach for studying protein behavior, but it requires enormous computational resources to obtain an adequate sampling of possible conformations. Recently, thanks to successes in predicting three-dimensional protein structures, there has been an explosion of research exploring the opportunities offered by deep learning to address the problem of protein conformational landscape. In this work, an artificial intelligence system based on a variant of the Transformer architecture is introduced and applied to the problem of determining the ensemble of three-dimensional structures that a protein can access and their statistical weight. After being trained on a dataset of conformations of a particular protein obtained using classical all-atom molecular dynamics, this neural network is able to directly generate physically plausible protein conformations similar to those obtained both through molecular dynamics and experimentally. The ordered sequence of conformations obtained as output of the neural network rapidly converges towards the most populated regions of the protein's conformational landscape, suggesting that the system may have learned not only the protein's three-dimensional organization but also the thermodynamic weights of the various feasible conformations. These features, combined with its simplicity and low computational load, make this Transformer variant an ideal candidate for the development of systems capable of performing generative molecular dynamics.

title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
shortTitle: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.

title: Unlocking Fine-Grained Cell Representations via Soft-Interior Rim Dense-Grid Pooling in Pathology Foundation Models
shortTitle: Unlocking Fine-Grained Cell Representations via Soft-Interior Rim Dense-Grid Pooling in Pathology Foundation Models
abstract: Fine-grained cell representations are essential for characterizing cellular heterogeneity and tissue organization in computational pathology. Pathology foundation models (PFMs) provide powerful pretrained features for transferable tissue analysis. HoVer-Net uses task-trained segmentation and typing, whereas CellViT++ averages native-grid tokens assigned to detected nuclei. However, the former requires cell-specific training; the latter ignores fractional nuclear coverage and can mix nuclear content with neighbouring tissue. Therefore, we propose SRDP, short for Soft-interior Rim Dense-grid Pooling, a training-free geometry-aware readout. We apply the frozen patch projection at half stride, interleave four offset lattices, map the cell mask to fractional coverage weights, and concatenate whole-cell pooling with two inner boundary pools. Across four datasets and six frozen encoders, SRDP improves mean balanced accuracy by 5.68 percentage points over native token averaging across 24 settings, including 11.22 points on average for CoNIC and Lizard. SRDP converts a coarse frozen PFM lattice into a mask-aligned, fine-grained cell representation without updating the encoder.

title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
shortTitle: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.

title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
shortTitle: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning

title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
shortTitle: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
abstract: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

title: A Think Block Is Conditioning, Not a Plan
shortTitle: A Think Block Is Conditioning, Not a Plan
abstract: Generative models increasingly write a chain of thought before drawing, and report large gains from doing so. We ask what that text contributes, by substitution rather than ablation: holding the generator, sampler and seeds fixed, we replace the think block with controlled alternatives and measure the image. Across a unified model with a think mode, a reinforcement-learned reasoning generator, and a planner driving a frozen diffusion model, the same picture emerges. Content-free prose of matched length is worth nothing or less ($-0.05$ to $-0.15$). One sentence from an unrelated 8B model, naming the subject and a few identifying details, matches the generator's own plan in three to six times fewer conditioning tokens. The value sits where the referent is in doubt: writing down a name is worth $+0.33$ when it is right and $+0.05$ when it is wrong, and where the generator already succeeds the whole effect is $-0.07 \pm 0.07$. Cutting a plan at the text encoder's window leaves 272 of 286 images byte-identical, and a plan rewritten to fit that window ties a bare identification ($+0.003 \pm 0.044$), so a plan contains nothing the identification does not already supply. Field-level interventions find only colour executed reliably, and a control writing the same sentences into the user prompt shows that limit belongs to the generator rather than to the planning channel. Two judges and two annotators replicate the central contrasts. A think block earns its keep as a specification of what to draw, not as a plan that is carried out.

title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
shortTitle: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
abstract: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.

title: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
shortTitle: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.

title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
shortTitle: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

title: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
shortTitle: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
abstract: Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built AttentionUNet-CA, which reads a 32 x 32 neighbourhood of land-cover states with four drivers (elevation, distance to major roads, distance to the central business district (CBD) and population density) and predicts the state of each cell ten years later. We tested it on Lucknow, India, with GLC_FCS30D land cover for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, a 30 m series mapped consistently over time, and compared its built-up class with GHSL and ESA WorldCover. AttentionUNet-CA was trained on 1990-2010, selected on held-out spatial blocks and evaluated once on 2010-2020, with three seeds. Baselines were the null model, a random-forest CA (RF-CA) and a U-Net CA without attention; each network was trained with and without class weights. Only 8.1% of the study area changed in the test decade, so no model matched the overall agreement of the null model (91.9%). On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
shortTitle: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

title: When Does Label-Free Deconfounding of Document Embeddings Work?
shortTitle: When Does Label-Free Deconfounding of Document Embeddings Work?
lab: Department of Computational Linguistics, University of Zurich / ETH Zurich / The University of Hong Kong
abstract: Document embeddings encode spurious attributes that can distort semantic comparisons; yet supervised erasure requires metadata that is often unavailable. We systematically investigate label-free deconfounding across corpora and embedding models. Our results show that label-free methods improve semantic utility over unprocessed embeddings, while simple geometric approaches recover much of the supervised benefit, sometimes matching metadata-supervised erasure in linear confounder recoverability and semantic utility. We identify two distinct causes of ineffective erasure: poor proxy-confounder alignment and insufficient intervention coverage. Crucially, confounder recoverability and semantic utility are distinct dimensions of deconfounding success: utility can improve despite residual confounder information, while stronger suppression does not necessarily improve utility. Moreover, reduced linear recoverability can coexist with substantial nonlinear recoverability. Together, these findings distinguish confounder discovery from intervention effectiveness and highlight the importance of evaluating nuisance suppression alongside semantic preservation.

title: HongguoTrending: A Longitudinal, Multimodal Archive of Trending Videos and Topics on a Leading Micro-Drama Platform
shortTitle: HongguoTrending: A Longitudinal, Multimodal Archive of Trending Videos and Topics on a Leading Micro-Drama Platform
abstract: Micro-dramas (duanju) are reshaping digital production and consumption, yet a lack of longitudinal data connecting series to their platform visibility persists, limiting our understanding of the emerging medium. We introduce HongguoTrending, a longitudinal, multimodal dataset of hourly snapshots from seven trending lists of Hongguo, China's largest micro-drama platform. Collected through a two-stage asynchronous pipeline, the archive links 63,200 ranking entries across 632 web list-hours and 157 client hours (889 distinct series) to metadata, cover images, sampled episode videos, and audience engagement metrics. Exploratory analyses show distinct turnover rates between web and mobile trending lists, production-driven mainstream values alongside kinship-centered synopses, genre-specific cover palettes, and strong associations between user sharing and next-day rank gains. Accessible via a RESTful API, this dataset supports empirical research on algorithmic gatekeeping, popularity dynamics, and multimodal digital culture.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
shortTitle: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

title: RETR: A Structure-Preserving RGB-Event Transformer for Robust 3D Lane Detection
shortTitle: RETR: A Structure-Preserving RGB-Event Transformer for Robust 3D Lane Detection
abstract: Robust 3D lane detection requires accurate metric road geometry recovery from visual inputs, yet conventional RGB-based approaches suffer from fragile lane evidence under adverse illumination, motion blur, and long-range perspective compression. Event cameras offer complementary high-temporal-resolution, high dynamic-range structural cues that are robust to these challenges, but their sparse, motion-dependent responses cannot be directly fused into consistent 3D geometry. In this paper, we present the first attempt to introduce event cameras into 3D lane detection. To enable systematic research, we first build two multimodal benchmarks with metric 3D lane annotations: DSEC-3DLD (real-world sequences) and Ev-OpenLane (large-scale simulated sequences). We further propose RETR, a structure preserving transformer that converts complementary RGB and event observations into coherent 3D lane geometry. RETR first aligns modality consistent evidence through Reciprocal Context Flow Fusion, then preserves thin and uncertain lane structures with Uncertainty Aware Structural Consolidation, and finally decodes ordered lane hypotheses using a Geometry State Decoder with proposal conditioned initialization, reference conditioned query evolution, and diversified geometric inquiry. Extensive experiments show that RETR achieves state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, especially showing strong improvements in challenging lighting and complex road geometry scenarios. Code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/duskswell/RETR.
