title: Cooperative Gradient Estimation for Multi-Robot Source Seeking with Heteroskedastic Measurements
shortTitle: Cooperative Gradient Estimation for Multi-Robot Source Seeking with Heteroskedastic Measurements
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for localizing the source of a three-dimensional scalar field using a team of heterogeneous cooperative mobile robots. Each robot measures the field intensity at its location and shares the information within the team. Measurement noise is explicitly considered, and heterogeneity arises from robot-dependent sensing accuracies, leading to heteroskedastic data. The proposed framework combines a weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellation-based formation strategy, defined on a spherical surface and parameterized by sensor noise variances, with a Weighted Least Squares estimator to compute the field gradient at the formation center. By explicitly accounting for sensor heterogeneity in both formation design and estimation, the method achieves robust gradient estimation under noisy measurements. In particular, we show analytically that this construction is nearly optimal. The covariance of the gradient estimate is derived in closed form, providing a lower bound on the attainable estimation variance for any formation on the sphere, and the proposed tessellation is shown to asymptotically satisfy the conditions under which this bound is attained. The estimated gradient is then exploited within a gradient-ascent strategy to guide the team toward the source location. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to alternative strategies and highlight its intrinsic ability to reconfigure online in response to robot failures, thereby enhancing its adaptability.

title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
shortTitle: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
abstract: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter $I$ (models, memory, skills) and a rule program $p_0$, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler $C_θ$ that maps structured tasks $g$ into new rule programs $p_g$. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one. title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
shortTitle: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
abstract: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

title: Evidence-Conditioned Completion and Synthesis of Electronic Health Records
shortTitle: Evidence-Conditioned Completion and Synthesis of Electronic Health Records
abstract: Patient information can guide electronic health record (EHR) generation, but how its amount shapes predictive utility and disclosure risk remains poorly characterized. We compared EHRDiB with three completion and eight synthesis methods on MIMIC-IV and numerical and discretized Duke Health representations. title: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
shortTitle: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
abstract: Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming. Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements.

title: Lesion-Aware Explainable AI for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading from Fundus Images
shortTitle: Lesion-Aware Explainable AI for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading from Fundus Images
abstract: Post-hoc explanations of deep-learning models for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are difficult to trust because different attribution methods highlight different retinal regions for the same image, and a visually plausible heatmap does not show that the highlighted pixels drive the prediction. We propose the Consensus-Calibrated Explanation Map (CCEM), which fuses Grad-CAM++, Ada-SISE, and SmoothGrad Integrated Gradients (SG-IG) using image-specific weights derived from annotation-free reliability cues: deletion sensitivity, inter-method agreement, compactness, retinal containment, and peak structure. CCEM explains a frozen ordinal grader, an EfficientNet-B7 with CBAM and a scalar regression head, pre-trained on EyePACS 2015 in Stage 1 and fine-tuned on APTOS 2019 in Stage 2 with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)-optimized thresholds; it reaches a QWK of 0.920 on the hidden Kaggle test set and 0.559 on the external MAPLES-DR cohort. Explanations are evaluated on MAPLES-DR, 198 MESSIDOR images with expert pixel-level lesion annotations that are never used for training, threshold fitting, or fusion. On the 193 images with annotated lesions, CCEM obtains the highest Soft Pointing Game score (69.61%; 95% CI 63.7-75.3), defined as the ratio of the strongest lesion-supported saliency to the global map maximum rather than a lesion detection rate, together with the lowest deletion AUC (0.570) and the best deletion-insertion balance (0.115); each gain is significant against the strongest single explainer on paired tests. Annotation-free, per-image reliability weighting therefore turns three disagreeing explainers into one map whose peak evidence is more lesion-supported and more faithful to the model than that of any single explainer.

title: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent
shortTitle: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent
abstract: When a production issue is reported, engineers get a description and some logs, but no failing test and no way to reproduce the fault. The logs show where the failure was noticed, not where it was caused: in 49% of the real reports we study, the text names none of the files that the fix later changed. We built a benchmark for this setting from two public datasets and 27 open-source projects (Apache, Red Hat, MongoDB, MariaDB, Qt and Sakai). It holds 38,001 resolved issue reports with their pasted logs, the code as it was while the bug was still present, and the files the fix changed. We present INQUEST, an agent that finds the faulty code using a 27B open-weights model. Code, not the model, controls the procedure. It first gathers the evidence, including the files fixed in similar past issues that were resolved before the report was filed. The model then makes only three bounded decisions: which files to open, what role each file plays in the failure, and how to rank them. On 26,544 evaluation reports, INQUEST ranks a changed file first for 68.6% and in the top five for 85.9%, names the correct module for 90.2%, and ranks a changed function first for 53.8%. On the reports that name no faulty file, it reaches 52.8% and 73.6%. A free agent loop with the same model and tools finds files equally well, but names the faulty function 14 points less often. On a 1,000-report sample, INQUEST beats our reimplementations of two published agents by 7 and 20 points of top-1 accuracy (4 and 16 counting only the reports those agents answered), and the same model used as a re-ranker by 6. We report the cost of every system and the results that go against us, and we release the benchmark, both systems and every run transcript.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
shortTitle: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
abstract: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
shortTitle: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $π_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.

title: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
shortTitle: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
shortTitle: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.

title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
shortTitle: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
abstract: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
shortTitle: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

title: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
shortTitle: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.

title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
shortTitle: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

title: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
shortTitle: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
abstract: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.

title: Consistency-Aware Map Generation at Multiple Zoom Levels Using Aerial Image
shortTitle: Consistency-Aware Map Generation at Multiple Zoom Levels Using Aerial Image
abstract: The multi-level tiled map service is widely used and serves as a kind of digital infrastructure. These map tiles are usually rendered from vector data, whose update needs to walk or drive with professional equipment to check every points of interest. This leads to inconvenience and expensive cost in timely updating maps. Compared with vector data, aerial images are much easier and cheaper to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-level map generation framework that can automatically generate accurate and consistent maps with multiple zoom levels from aerial images. It consists of a level-aware map generator and a consistency-aware map generator. The level-aware map generator is able to generate accurate initial maps with realistic details for each zoom level. The consistency-aware map generator regards initial maps at each zoom level as a sequence and builds the connection between them, so as to guarantee content consistency between maps at different zoom levels. Furthermore, we collect a large-scale high-quality dataset called Multi-Level Map (MLM) for map generation at multiple zoom levels. Experiments on our MLM dataset show that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art map generation methods on both comprehensive quantitative metrics and perceptual quality.

title: ElevatorII: High-Performance Fully-Static Cross-ISA Binary Translation
shortTitle: ElevatorII: High-Performance Fully-Static Cross-ISA Binary Translation
abstract: The established method for running software compiled for one instruction-set architecture (ISA) on a different ISA is by emulation in conjunction with just-in-time (JIT) compilation. This requires run-time support on the target that needs to be trusted and whose compilation decisions are hard to predict or reconstruct. We present ElevatorII, a fully static, ahead-of-time cross-ISA binary-to-binary compiler from x86 to AArch64 that challenges the established consensus. Our approach eliminates the need for run-time support on the target, removes the hard to reproduce effects of dynamic compilation, and provides the capability to exhaustively test the actual binary that is eventually executed. Our approach combines superset disassembly with observation-guided path selection. Superset disassembly overcomes the code vs. data differentiation problem by creating a separate control flow path for every possible interpretation of every byte in the input binary. It guarantees that there is pre-translated code for every possible jump destination in the original text segment, even for computed jumps that are not statically decidable. Static and observation-guided path selection then creates additional optimized "confirmed code paths" that overlay the regular grid. On the 11 SPEC CPU 2026 Integer benchmarks that do not use C++ exceptions, ElevatorII runs at 2.5x native AArch64 time, on par with Box64, the fastest dynamic translator, and 5x faster than QEMU. It also translates binaries obfuscated with virtualization and branch functions, which no static disassembler can follow. Our approach trades execution performance for space: our output code is 51x the size of code compiled from source. We alleviate this by separating cold code to a .text.unlikely ELF section: only 2-3% hot code winds up in the main ELF section, while the rest will likely never be loaded into memory.

title: EndoComparer: Comparative Surgical Video Question Answering with Pseudo-Siamese Visual Adaptation and Perceive-then-Compare Reasoning
shortTitle: EndoComparer: Comparative Surgical Video Question Answering with Pseudo-Siamese Visual Adaptation and Perceive-then-Compare Reasoning
abstract: Purpose: Surgical training benefits from explicit comparison between cases: in patient condition, in technique and in skill proficiency. Surgical vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising and flexible interface for this purpose. Yet current VLMs typically see one video at a time, and they often fall short when asked to compare videos. Methods: We propose EndoComparer, a VLM for comparative surgical video question answering with two components. (a) A Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA (PSVL) gives each video slot its own low-rank adapter over a shared frozen vision encoder, separating the two videos in the visual pathway at the cost of a single encoder pass. (b) A Perceive-then-Compare chain of thought (PtC-CoT) trains the model to first state what each video shows, then derive the answer from these statements. We further curate EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice questions on video-pair over cholecystectomy and gastric bypass procedures, covering anatomy, tool, action and skill. Results: EndoComparer outperforms strong generalist and surgical VLMs on detecting and specifying difference between videos. Ablations show that two proposed components contribute complimentarily, and the model remains more robust under a video-swap control that exposes confusion between the two videos. Conclusion: Providing a dedicated visual reasoning path through PSVL and PtC-CoT makes cross-case comparison of surgical videos more robust for VLMs. EndoDiffVQA and EndoComparer provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for this task. title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
shortTitle: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
abstract: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
shortTitle: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
abstract: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
shortTitle: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
abstract: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

title: Learning Spatially Aware Audio-Visual Features from Videos with Mono Audio
shortTitle: Learning Spatially Aware Audio-Visual Features from Videos with Mono Audio
abstract: Comprehensive audio-visual perception requires both semantic and spatial reasoning. Existing spatial models suffer from poor generalization due to data scarcity, while semantic-only models fail to capture spatial characteristics completely. We introduce a model capable of jointly reasoning over binaural audio and vision on semantic and spatial tasks with improved generalization. To overcome the shortage in real-world data, we develop an automatic pipeline that localizes the sound source in a video, estimates its relative 3D trajectory, and renders binaural audio. We then use this to spatialize VGGSound, allowing us to train at a much larger scale. We demonstrate improved performance and generalization on spatial reasoning tasks while still remaining competitive on semantic tasks compared to semantic-only models.

title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
shortTitle: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
abstract: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints. We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure. NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

title: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
shortTitle: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
abstract: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. NAP-Wave is trained on a physics-informed loss built from the Lippmann-Schwinger integral equation, so no differentiation of the network with respect to its input is required. We develop a decoupled optimization strategy in which Adam updates the parameters of the neural plane-wave basis, while the linear combination coefficients are computed exactly by a least-squares (LS) solver. We couple this with an adaptive-depth training strategy in which the network starts shallow and grows progressively layer-by-layer. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. To ensure reproducibility, the code is available at https://github.com/Hamza-Kamil/NAP-WAVE.

title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
shortTitle: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure

H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
shortTitle: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

title: Towards Probabilistically Safe Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Deployment on Humanoid and Aerial Robots
shortTitle: Towards Probabilistically Safe Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Deployment on Humanoid and Aerial Robots
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire complex skills, but standard RL formulations do not guarantee that learned policies satisfy safety constraints, which limits their use in safety-critical settings. Existing safe RL methods with provable guarantees typically support only restricted classes of constraints and require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions, which prevents their direct integration with state-of-the-art algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). In this paper, we extend the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to overcome these limitations. Our formulation accommodates a general class of trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability, and our analysis allows for biased value and gradient estimators. We show that, with high probability, the constraint violation throughout training is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, and decays to this level if the initial policy is unsafe. We also establish the convergence properties of the iterates to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Finally, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with PPO-style estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.

title: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
shortTitle: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
abstract: A dynamic quantum circuit measures qubits during a run and chooses later operations from the outcomes. These branches make the qubits wait: the outcome must reach the classical controller, and the controller must decide. We present qlin, a compiler that reduces this waiting time. qlin moves operations out of branches without delaying the program, a property proved in Lean 4. For error-correction decoders, which branch on syndromes that are almost always zero, qlin compiles the likely syndromes into one multiway branch and keeps the original program for the rest. A cost model decides when a classically controlled gate should become a quantum-controlled gate instead. On all benchmarks, qlin checks that the compiled program computes what its source computes, and the checker is proved sound in Lean 4. At the published per-decision cost of the QICK controller (42 ns), 10 of 65 programs run at least 10% faster than the best baseline in our cost model, up to 91.2%, mostly because one multiway branch replaces a long chain of if statements. On the register-transfer logic of the QubiC controller, a compiled distance-5 repetition decoder selects its correction in 21.3 instead of 151.1 expected cycles. Timing runs on an IBM device were too noisy to confirm or reject the model's ranking.

title: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
shortTitle: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
abstract: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.

title: Data-Driven Heuristic-Guided Business Process Redesign
shortTitle: Data-Driven Heuristic-Guided Business Process Redesign
abstract: Business process redesign (BPR) has a long-standing catalog of best-practice redesign heuristics, yet, applying them remains a mostly manual task that requires extensive domain knowledge. Despite recent advances using Large Language Models (LLMs) for conversational process model redesign, limitations remain. For example, redesign is user-driven instead of data-driven and is not guided by best practices such as the redesign heuristics. Moreover, only one change can be handled at a time. To address these limitations, given an event log and a BPMN model, we present the DH-BPR framework to realize data-driven heuristic-guided BPR using LLMs. To design DH-BPR, we first conducted an analysis of which redesign heuristics can be automatically detected and applied given information contained in an event log such as the fraction of cases that bypass an activity. Based on this, DH-BPR detects and validates heuristic candidates through a combination of rule-based techniques and an LLM. After that, DH-BPR jointly designs and records an application plan for valid candidates, before finally yielding a redesigned BPMN model and an updated resource model (the way resources execute the process). Evaluation based on simulation using a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs shows that the framework's redesign reduces the mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.

title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
shortTitle: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
abstract: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
shortTitle: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
abstract: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

title: Where slide-level foundation-model classifiers fail on atypical breast lesions
shortTitle: Where slide-level foundation-model classifiers fail on atypical breast lesions
abstract: Whether a ductal breast lesion is called atypical hyperplasia or low-grade carcinoma in situ increasingly determines surgery. However, slide-level classifiers built on pathology foundation models (PFMs) perform worst on these lesions. Using four PFMs, cross-validation on BRACS and preregistered hypotheses, we studied where the classification of atypia fails. Because slides are labelled with their most severe lesion, only 39% of the slides with annotated atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) were labelled ADH. Attention ranked the lesion high but rarely first, and showing the model only the lesion helped little, whereas classifiers trained per decision with lesion-level labels improved all four atypical boundaries. ADH regions inserted into benign slides raised the probability of malignancy more than that of atypia. In a hospital with pathologist-labelled single-subtype slides and in HISTAI, benign slides were scored closer to lesions and triage specificity fell from 0.48-0.53 to 0.00-0.07 and 0.22.

title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
shortTitle: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

title: Floorplan-Context-Aware Cross-Environment Human Activity Recognition from mmWave Radar Point Clouds
shortTitle: Floorplan-Context-Aware Cross-Environment Human Activity Recognition from mmWave Radar Point Clouds
abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) models based on mmWave radar point clouds and trained in controlled open spaces often experience performance degradation when deployed in furnished rooms. We propose a Floorplan-Context-Aware (FCA) HAR enhancement method that augments the input with subject-furniture relative position information to improve cross-environment performance. Because existing mmWave point-cloud datasets lack registered floorplans, we introduce a pseudo-landmark augmentation strategy for training the FCA model. In cross-environment evaluation on the mm-ADL-Home dataset, FCA achieves 77.70% accuracy and 65.49% macro-F1, improving upon the point-cloud-only direct-transfer baseline by 10.73 and 10.05 percentage points, respectively, and exceeding the strongest evaluated adaptation baseline by 7.37 and 6.27 percentage points. At deployment, FCA requires only a one-time registration of furniture landmarks, with no target-domain activity annotations or model weight updates.

title: Beyond the Training Cameras: Coverage-Controlled Probes of Viewing Direction in Frozen Vision Models
shortTitle: Beyond the Training Cameras: Coverage-Controlled Probes of Viewing Direction in Frozen Vision Models
abstract: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world. Do their hidden features encode the direction from which the camera views a scene, and if so, in what form? We study the relative viewing direction $α$ of two objects in rendered scenes where both object centres stay at fixed pixels while the camera moves, so that perspective, shading and shadows change but the projected layout does not. In eight pretrained models, from diffusion models to self-supervised and image-text encoders, $α$ is encoded in a strikingly simple form: a single two-dimensional plane in the hidden space, shared across scenes, in which the difference between the two objects' features traces $(\cosα, \sinα)$. The plane keeps its orientation when lighting, colours, floors and object shapes change. This encoding is more than a summary of a few visible measurements: readouts fitted on one set of camera paths stay accurate at camera positions outside their range in seven of the eight models, whereas decoders of the measured object and shadow geometry, equally accurate within that range, fail there. In the diffusion transformer PixArt-$α$, the plane forms abruptly at a single block and carries direction information to later blocks, yet editing it changes the objects rather than the generated viewpoint. We also examine how this encoding carries over to scanned real objects.

title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
shortTitle: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
abstract: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
shortTitle: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
shortTitle: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
abstract: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
shortTitle: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
abstract: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $dσ^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $σ^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
shortTitle: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
shortTitle: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

title: PSK: A Matrix-Free Single-Loop Method for K-Level Physics-Based Control
shortTitle: PSK: A Matrix-Free Single-Loop Method for K-Level Physics-Based Control
abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over $K$ steps as $K$-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min--max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop $K$-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an $ε$-stationary control in $O(ε^{-3})$ iterations, with a $K$-independent exponent but a $K$-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz--John, and PSK keeps the $O(ε^{-3})$ complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $ε$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $Ω(ε^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/ε$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.

title: When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
shortTitle: When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
abstract: AI agents often discover mid-execution that their plan is broken, for example when an action fails or a tool is withdrawn. Deployed systems use conventions such as retry loops or "always replan," and a recent benchmark finds no fixed strategy dominates. This paper derives the optimal policy. In the model, a disruption destroys the causal support of part of a plan; repair is a partial reset that preserves the plan's structure, replanning is a full reset, and changing a plan is costly because others have conditioned on it. The optimal policy is a threshold in effective disruption depth: repair shallow damage, replan after deep damage, and abandon the goal when even a fresh plan is not worth its cost. Depth depends on plan structure. In expectation, a single broken action forces 1+R(G)/n actions to be revalidated, where R(G) counts the pairs of actions joined by a dependency path; to first order, a fully serial plan switches to replanning at raw damage about w times smaller than a plan of w parallel chains. A closed-form stability-price threshold determines when a worse repaired plan should be kept over a better fresh one. As language-model planners push replanning costs toward zero, the stability price becomes the only force sustaining plan commitment. Under repeated disruptions, revision frictions make commitment hysteresis optimal: the agent keeps executing a plan it would never choose fresh, and each repair adds patch debt until the debt outweighs repair's cost advantage and the agent rebuilds. A value-of-diagnosis result states when measuring damage is worth its compute and shows that "always replan" is optimal when damage is predictably deep and replanning is the better fallback. A separately implemented numerical checker tests each proposition (zero violations; 1.6 million static-model evaluations), and the model's regime map reproduces that benchmark's regime flips qualitatively.

title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
shortTitle: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
abstract: In edge-cloud collaborative inference, the layers of a deep neural network (DNN) are placed on edge and cloud virtual machines (VMs) for every request, while the edge load and the cross-cloud bandwidth change over time. We propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework that scores each layer-VM pair by end-to-end delay and energy and places the layers one at a time on the best-scoring VM. Such greedy placement is myopic when trained on per-layer labels: offloading to the cloud slows the first offloaded layer while the gain appears only in later layers, so the policy keeps too many requests at the edge. Training on the remaining request time after each decision removes this myopia and reduces the mean delay by 12-56% on congested workloads. In CloudSimSDN simulations with three DNNs and two public request traces, IA-MoE has the lowest mean delay of all compared methods on congested VGG16 workloads, across cross-cloud bandwidths of 150-600 Mbps, fluctuating bandwidth and saturated edge servers. A random forest trained on the same label is 5-27% slower, and only a heuristic that sends whole requests to the cloud uses less energy, at up to 20 times the delay. When the edge is lightly loaded, offloading does not pay and simple heuristics perform as well. IA-MoE also beats a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent with the same features in all 19 tested settings, with a mean delay lower by a factor of 1.3 to 10.5, and trains in minutes instead of hours.

title: Chimera: A Configurable LLM Decode Accelerator Architecture with Compute-Memory-Floorplan Co-Design for HBM-Equipped Multi-Die FPGAs
shortTitle: Chimera: A Configurable LLM Decode Accelerator Architecture with Compute-Memory-Floorplan Co-Design for HBM-Equipped Multi-Die FPGAs
abstract: GPUs are widely used for LLM inference, but single-request decoding is memory-bound, leaving their compute underutilized while they draw substantial power. HBM-equipped FPGAs are well suited to LLM decoding: their customizable datapaths use memory bandwidth more energy-efficiently than GPUs. However, high memory bandwidth alone does not ensure high decode performance: exploiting it requires parallel compute and memory interfaces, whose resource costs and placement on the chip can limit the throughput. We present Chimera, a configurable LLM decode accelerator architecture that co-designs compute, memory access, and floorplan. Specifically, HBM Proxy Ports extend HBM access to compute lanes on every super logic region (SLR) die, and tiered expert storage holds mixture-of-experts weights beyond the HBM capacity. In addition, a unified configuration analysis estimates per-token latency and per-SLR resource use and guides the design of each configuration within resource budgets. On an AMD Alveo U280, we build ten designs for eight dense, mixture-of-experts, hybrid linear/standard-attention, and ternary LLMs, up to an 80B-parameter mixture-of-experts LLM on four memory tiers. Chimera's designs achieve a geometric mean of 1.6$\times$ the token throughput of prior state-of-the-art FPGA implementations and 3.0$\times$ and 1.5$\times$ the energy efficiency of the RTX 3090 and A100 GPUs, setting a new benchmark for LLM decoding on HBM-equipped FPGAs.

title: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
shortTitle: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
abstract: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at https://github.com/yasirmahmud/RTLReviewBench
